issues.where: 6-snowflake §6.6: fig-6d (fig/1440-light-fig-6d.png, fig/390-dark-fig-6d.png), the paragraph after it (sweep/1440-light/6-snowflake/011.png) and Check yourself Q2
issues.problem: Fig 6·d, its caption and Check-yourself answer 2 say Discord uses 'the same 41 bits' from 2015, lasting to about 2084. The very next paragraph says Discord's documentation specifies a 42-bit timestamp, which from 2015 lasts to about 2154. The page contradicts itself across two adjacent blocks.
issues.fix: Keep the figure's teaching point (same bit width, later epoch = more years) but label the lower line 'epoch 2015' without '(discord)', and say in the caption that Discord's docs count 42 bits (the sign bit included), which stretches it further. Alternatively, reconcile in one sentence in the paragraph: Twitter's layout is also 42 bits if you count the unused top bit; kept positive in a signed 64-bit integer, both effectively get 41. Make answer 2 match whichever you choose.

issues.problem: The prose narrates the recording and the teacher instead of stating things, which is lec01's issue 14 again. Examples: '(The recording garbles the lecture's exact words here; that reflex is the sense of it.)'; 'When someone tells the instructor their database is slow, the first thing he checks…'; 'the team that built Amazon's ID service sat right next to him'; 'In 2016, bored at Amazon and heavily into MongoDB, the instructor wrote…'; 'the class board crossed it out at the crash, and the lecture counted both 8 and 9 as leaked'; 'One idea raised in class'; 'The lecture describes it as living on the heap'; 'As worked out in class'; the fig-3-2 label 'strictly monotonic, as the lecture says it'.
issues.fix: Delete the recording-garbled aside. Rewrite teacher biography as plain claims ('A common first check for a slow database is index size'; 'Amazon described the design in a public tech talk'; 'A 2016 benchmark (arpitbhayani.me) measured…'). Change 'raised in class' to 'One tempting idea'. Leave provenance to the meta lines and the 'Redrawn from the class board' captions. Relabel fig-3-2 as 'strictly monotonic'.

issues.problem: §3.5 tells the four-clocks story three times in a row with almost no prose between: the pause-and-think card (23, 24, 23, 23 → 232, 244, 237, 239), then Clip 3·1 with the same numbers, one sentence, then fig-3d, a step-through captioned 'the clip's static twin' with the same four steps. That is the 'stack of components without prose' the sample forbids. §2.6 repeats the pattern with Clip 2·1, then fig-2d (static twin of the same flush/crash), then a pause card on the same 6+3+1 answer.
issues.fix: Keep one moving and one static telling per story, at most. Either drop fig-3d and fig-2d (the 'clip as text' already serves readers who can't play the clip), or keep the step-through and show the clip only when the reader asks for it. Put a real paragraph between the pause card and the clip, for example the 'why' that lets the reader check their answer.

issues.problem: The 64-digit binary string is packed edge to edge. The leading 0 sits on the border of the unused-bit cell, digits touch the 41|10 and 10|12 dividers, and the digits render at about 11px, under the 12px floor. It reads as a smudge rather than three fields. The phone redraw (fields only) is fine.
issues.fix: Group the bits by field with at least 4px of padding inside each cell. Either use nibble spacing at 12px or more, or drop the full binary at desktop too and show the field values (time 362…, machine 7, counter 0) as on the phone, with the binary as an optional line below.

issues.problem: The '1 GB' and '~4 GB' labels sit next to whole index entries (user_id + id), so the figure says the index grows 4×. With a 4-byte user_id the entry goes from 8 to 20 bytes, about 2.5×; only the id column grows 4×. The footnote ('~4× vs a 4-byte INT') is about the column, not the entry, so the label and the footnote disagree.
issues.fix: Label the id cells '4 B' and '16 B' and the entries '8 B → 20 B per entry (~2.5×)', or drop the GB numbers. Keep the footnote about the column.

issues.fix: Say 'm1-09 is never handed out' and drop the clause about 8, or say explicitly that it differs from the drawn example.

issues.problem: The flush uses the key's dashed 'async copy (head on whoever starts it)' glyph with the head on the disk, but the machine starts the flush. By the course key that reads as the disk pulling.
issues.fix: Draw the flush as a solid write arrow memory → disk (the machine is pushing a write), keeping dashed async copy for replication only.
